conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the core clinical skill in anorectal/perianal disease, and what are the dangerous mimics that can't be missed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: The skill is taking an anorectal complaint and placing it correctly — the benign causes overlap. Can't-miss dangerous mimics: colorectal cancer (bleeding) and Crohn's disease (fistulae/abscesses) — always exclude these.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What three triage questions split the whole anorectal disease group?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Painful or painless?
  • Bleeding or discharge?
  • Lump or no lump?

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: On the triage table, what are the pain, bleeding, discharge and lump features of haemorrhoids?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Pain: painless (unless thrombosed).
  • Bleeding: bright red, on surface.
  • Discharge: mucus.
  • Lump: prolapsing.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: On the triage table, what are the features of an anal fissure (pain, bleeding, lump)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Pain: very painful (on defecation).
  • Bleeding: bright red, small.
  • Lump: sentinel tag.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: On the triage table, what are the features of a perianal abscess (pain, lump)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Pain: painful, throbbing.
  • Lump: tender fluctuant lump.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: On the triage table, what are the features of fistula-in-ano (pain, discharge, lump)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Pain: mild/none.
  • Discharge: persistent discharge.
  • Lump: external opening.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: On the triage table, what are the features of a pilonidal sinus (pain, discharge, lump)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Pain: painful if infected.
  • Discharge: discharge.
  • Lump: natal cleft.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the shared exam approach for anorectal disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Inspection — perianal skin, prolapse, external openings, skin tags.
  • DRE — tone, masses, tenderness.
  • Proctoscopy — for haemorrhoids; a suspected fissure is often too painful to tolerate it, so the diagnosis is clinical and examination is deferred to EUA if needed.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: Why is an anal fissure often difficult to examine, and what does that tell you?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: A fissure is often too painful to examine without anaesthesia — the pain itself is diagnostic.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the abscess → fistula cross-cutting principle?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Fistula formation occurs through chronic infection of the anal crypt glands — an abscess forms, then discharges pus via the skin, leaving a tract. The same cryptoglandular process, acute vs chronic.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the Crohn's association cross-cutting principle in anorectal disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Perianal disease (especially fistulae + abscesses) is a classic Crohn's feature — recurrent/complex/multiple perianal disease should prompt thinking about IBD.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are haemorrhoids, and what is the normal function of the structure involved?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Abnormal swelling/enlargement of the anal vascular cushions (which normally help the sphincter maintain continence).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: Where are the three haemorrhoidal cushions located, and what is the peak age?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: At 3, 7 and 11 o'clock (lithotomy position); peak age 45–65.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: How do internal vs external haemorrhoids differ in pain and innervation?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Internal (above dentate line): painless — visceral innervation; prolapse & bleed.
  • External (below dentate line): can be painful — somatic innervation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the degree (grading) classification of haemorrhoids?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• 1st: bleed but do not prolapse.
  • 2nd: prolapse on defecation, spontaneously reduce.
  • 3rd: prolapse, require digital reduction.
  • 4th: persistently prolapsed.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the risk factors for haemorrhoids?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Excessive straining (chronic constipation)
  • increasing age
  • raised intra-abdominal pressure (pregnancy, chronic cough, ascites).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the clinical features of haemorrhoids?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Painless bright red rectal bleeding after defecation, on paper or covering the pan
  • mucus discharge
  • pruritus
  • rectal fullness/lump
  • soiling
Large prolapsed haemorrhoids can thrombose — very painful, acute purple/blue, oedematous, tense, tender mass.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the typical bleeding pattern in haemorrhoids, and how far does it take you?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Haemorrhoidal blood is on the surface of the stool / on the paper, not mixed in; blood mixed through the stool points to cancer. This is supportive, not decisive — low rectal tumours also bleed bright red onto the surface, so rectal bleeding is always assessed on its own merits.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What investigations are used for haemorrhoids?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Proctoscopy confirms; FBC + clotting if significant bleeding/anaemia. Seeing haemorrhoids does not end the assessment: rectal bleeding is triaged with FIT and lower GI investigation where indicated (NICE); colonoscopy is also used to exclude concurrent pathology before surgery.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: How are haemorrhoids managed conservatively and which degrees get rubber-band ligation?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Most managed conservatively: increase fibre + fluid, laxatives, topical analgesia (lignocaine gel — short courses of a few days only, as it sensitises anal skin (BNF)).
  • Thrombosed: analgesia, ice packs and stool softeners, settling over 1–2 weeks; if severe and presenting within 72 h of onset, refer urgently for consideration of surgical excision (NICE).
  • 1st–3rd degree → rubber-band ligation (or injection sclerotherapy) if conservative measures fail (NICE).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the surgical options for haemorrhoids and their complications?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• HAL/THD (Doppler-guided artery ligation) for 2nd/3rd
  • haemorrhoidectomy for 3rd/4th (Milligan-Morgan or stapled)
Complications of surgery: recurrence, anal stricturing, faecal incontinence.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: Which analgesia should be avoided in haemorrhoids and why?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Avoid opioid analgesia — it worsens constipation and the underlying problem.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is an anal fissure, and how are acute vs chronic distinguished?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: A tear in the lining of the anal canal below the dentate line — sharp anal pain on defecation and bleeding. Acute (<6 weeks) vs chronic (≥6 weeks); chronic develops the triad of fissure + sentinel skin tag + hypertrophied anal papilla.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the location clue for an anal fissure, and what does an atypical location suggest?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Posterior midline in the vast majority (poorest blood supply). Lateral/multiple/otherwise atypical fissures → think a secondary cause (Crohn's, malignancy, infection). An anterior midline fissure is the second commonest primary site and is commoner in women, particularly after childbirth — not itself a red flag.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the risk factors for an anal fissure?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Constipation/hard stool (the main one), low fibre
  • secondary causes — IBD, infection.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the clinical features of an anal fissure?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Intense, sharp/tearing pain on defecation (lasts hours after)
  • bright red bleeding (small volume, on paper)
  • the patient is often too tender for DRE/proctoscopy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the conservative first-line management of an anal fissure?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Fibre + fluids
  • stool softeners/laxatives
  • topical analgesia (short courses only (BNF))
  • sitz baths.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the role of topical GTN in an anal fissure, and the next step if refractory?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
Topical GTN relaxes the internal sphincter → improves blood flow → heals. 0.4% rectal GTN is the only licensed UK option, applied for 6–8 weeks; diltiazem is used off-label when GTN is not tolerated (BNF). Refer to colorectal surgery if pain has not resolved by 6–8 weeks (NICE). Refractory:
  • botulinum toxin injection
  • lateral internal sphincterotomy (definitive but small risk of incontinence).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is the classic side effect of topical GTN in fissure treatment?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Headache — a common reason for poor adherence.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is a perianal abscess, and where does the infection start?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: A localised collection of pus; ~90% arise from cryptoglandular gland infection at the dentate line (ACPGBI) — when a gland is blocked, infection starts in the intersphincteric space and then spreads, most often downward to the perianal space. Twice as common in men.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: How are perianal abscesses classified by location, and which is commonest?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Perianal (commonest)
  • then ischiorectal
  • intersphincteric
  • supralevator.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the clinical features of a perianal abscess?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Painful
  • throbbing
  • tender fluctuant perianal lump
  • erythema
  • ± fever/systemic upset.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: If no abscess is visible and DRE isn't possible due to pain/sphincter spasm, what should you suspect?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: An intersphincteric abscess or anal fissure.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What investigations are used for a perianal abscess?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: If an abscess is clearly present, no further investigations are required before treatment; MRI/EUA for complex/recurrent disease (to define tracts).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: How is a perianal abscess managed, and what is the red-flag complication?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: Surgical drainage within 24h (RCS) — especially urgent in diabetes, systemic sepsis or immunocompromise. Drainage is the treatment: antibiotics do not drain an abscess and are not indicated in a routine uncomplicated perianal abscess (ACPGBI) — reserve them for surrounding cellulitis, systemic sepsis, diabetes or immunocompromise. Red flag: Fournier's gangrene — necrotising perineal infection, a surgical emergency.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is a fistula-in-ano, and what is the abscess link?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: A chronic abnormal epithelial-lined tract connecting the anorectal lumen (internal opening) to the perineal/buttock skin (external opening). It follows chronic cryptoglandular infection — an abscess that discharges leaves a fistula tract, which follows in a substantial minority of cases.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the clinical features of a fistula-in-ano?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Persistent perianal discharge (pus/blood/faeculent)
  • recurrent abscesses
  • an external opening on inspection ± a palpable cord.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is Goodsall's rule for fistula-in-ano?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• An anterior external opening → tracks radially/straight to the anal canal
  • a posterior one → tracks in a curved path to the posterior midline
In practice the rule is an unreliable guide — EUA ± MRI defines the tract.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What investigations are used for a fistula-in-ano?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• MRI pelvis (to map the tract, especially complex/Crohn's)
  • EUA.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: How is a fistula-in-ano managed (fistulotomy vs seton)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Fistulotomy: lay open low/simple tracts.
  • Seton: for high tracts crossing significant sphincter (preserve continence) — especially Crohn's-related fistulae.
Treat the underlying Crohn's if present.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What is a pilonidal sinus, and who is the typical patient?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back: A hair-containing sinus tract in the natal cleft (sacrococcygeal) — hair penetrates the skin and drives a foreign-body reaction. Typical patient: young, hirsute male; sedentary/prolonged sitting.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: What are the clinical features of a pilonidal sinus?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Intermittent natal-cleft discharge/swelling
  • presents acutely as a painful pilonidal abscess
  • visible midline pits.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.front: How is a pilonidal sinus managed (acute, chronic, conservative)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.back:
• Acute abscess: incision + drainage.
  • Chronic/recurrent: excision of the sinus tracts + hygiene/hair-removal advice.
  • Conservative: keep the area clean and dry, with hair removal (depilatory cream, waxing or laser) — razor shaving of the natal cleft is associated with recurrence and is not advised.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What is intestinal ischaemia, and what is the decisive fork?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Inadequate blood flow through mesenteric vessels → bowel ischaemia. The decisive fork: chronic (atherosclerotic, "intestinal angina") vs acute (sudden occlusion, a surgical emergency).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Which three arteries supply the gut, and what does each supply?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back:
• Coeliac → foregut (rarely ischaemic — rich collaterals)
  • SMA → midgut (distal duodenum to splenic flexure; the key vessel in acute ischaemia)
  • IMA → hindgut (splenic flexure to rectum).
The watershed is the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA border).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Why is the coeliac territory rarely ischaemic?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: It supplies the foregut and has rich collaterals.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Compare the mechanism of chronic vs acute mesenteric ischaemia.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Chronic: atherosclerosis gradually narrows vessels. Acute: sudden occlusion, usually of the SMA — though NOMI is a low-flow state with no clot, and MVT is venous.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Compare the key risk factor of chronic vs acute mesenteric ischaemia.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Chronic: CVD profile (age, smoking, DM, HTN). Acute: AF (LA thrombus → embolises to SMA).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Compare the pain of chronic vs acute mesenteric ischaemia.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Chronic: postprandial colicky ("intestinal angina"). Acute: constant, out of proportion to exam.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What happens if chronic and acute mesenteric ischaemia are left untreated?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Chronic: weight loss, food avoidance. Acute: necrosis → perforation → death.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What is the classic triad of chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back:
• Postprandial central colicky pain (~30 min after eating)
  • weight loss (food avoidance + malabsorption)
  • and an abdominal bruit.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Why do symptoms of chronic mesenteric ischaemia appear only with advanced disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: ≥2 of the 3 vessels usually have to be significantly stenosed before symptoms appear — collateral supply compensates.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What investigations are used in chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Routine bloods are often normal; check the CV risk profile. CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: How is chronic mesenteric ischaemia managed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back:
• Modify CV risk factors (smoking, DM, HTN)
  • statin + antiplatelet (secondary prevention)
  • endovascular 1st-line (percutaneous mesenteric angioplasty + stenting)
  • open surgery (endarterectomy/bypass) if endovascular fails.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What is the commonest subtype of acute mesenteric ischaemia, and its distinguishing clue?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Embolic (commonest) — a clot from elsewhere lodges in the SMA. Distinguishing clue: AF, recent MI; sudden onset, no prior history.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Describe the thrombotic subtype of acute mesenteric ischaemia.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Acute-on-chronic atherosclerosis of the SMA. Distinguishing clue: a preceding chronic mesenteric ischaemia history.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Describe non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: A low-flow state with no physical clot. Distinguishing clue: shock, sepsis, heart failure, vasopressors.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: Describe the venous subtype of acute mesenteric ischaemia (MVT).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Mesenteric vein thrombosis. Distinguishing clue: a younger patient, thrombophilia, slower onset.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What is the cardinal clinical clue of acute mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Acute pain out of proportion to examination findings. Also nausea, vomiting, progression to shock/peritonitis/sepsis, and look for an embolic source (AF, valve disease).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What investigations are used in acute mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: FBC, U&E, clotting, amylase, LFT. ABG: metabolic acidosis + raised lactate (a marker of ischaemic tissue). CT angiography is definitive (vessel occlusion ± bowel changes).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: How is acute mesenteric ischaemia managed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back:
• IV resuscitation
  • broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (faecal contamination risk)
  • emergency surgery — revascularise (thrombectomy/embolectomy) and resect non-viable bowel, restoring flow first because marginal bowel can recover once reperfused
  • second-look laparotomy at 24–48h to reassess bowel viability.
Subtype matters: venous (MVT) is anticoagulation-led, and NOMI is treated by correcting the low-flow state.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What is the prognosis of acute mesenteric ischaemia, and what is essential?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Mortality is high if bowel necrosis occurs. Early CT and urgent surgery are essential.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What is ischaemic colitis, and where are the watershed areas?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back: Acute, transient compromise of blood flow to the large bowel (not the small bowel). The watershed area is the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA border). The rectum is usually spared because of its dual blood supply. Usually self-limiting; rarely progresses to necrosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What are the features, investigations, and management of ischaemic colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back:
• Features: lower-left abdominal pain + bloody diarrhoea
  • CT/AXR: thumbprinting (mucosal oedema); colonoscopy confirms
  • Management: conservative — IV fluids, antibiotics, bowel rest; surgery only for gangrene/perforation/stricture.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.front: What is the key contrast between acute mesenteric ischaemia and ischaemic colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.back:
• Acute mesenteric ischaemia = SMA, small bowel, catastrophic, emergency surgery
  • Ischaemic colitis = IMA/watershed, large bowel, usually self-limiting, conservative.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is coeliac disease, and what is the basic consequence?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: An autoimmune sensitivity to gluten → immune-mediated mucosal damage → villous atrophy + malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the trigger in coeliac disease, and where is it found?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Gluten (the gliadin fraction), found in wheat, barley, and rye.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: Describe the autoimmune mucosal damage in coeliac disease.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: A T-cell-mediated response (HLA-DQ2/DQ8) → villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: How does coeliac disease lead to malabsorption, and which nutrients are affected?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Reduced absorptive surface → malabsorption. Iron, folate, B12, calcium, and fat-soluble vitamins are all affected.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the genetic link in coeliac disease, and what autoimmune cluster does it share associations with?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: A strong genetic link: HLA-DQ2 (95%) and HLA-DQ8. It clusters with the autoimmune group — T1DM, thyroid disease, and Addison's. Offer coeliac serology at diagnosis in type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease, and to first-degree relatives (NICE).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What are the GI symptoms of coeliac disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Chronic/intermittent diarrhoea (often steatorrhoea — pale, fatty, floating), bloating, abdominal distension, cramping, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss / failure to thrive (in children).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the commonest presenting clue of coeliac disease in adults?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Unexplained anaemia — iron ± folate ± B12. It is the commonest presenting clue in adults.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What malabsorption consequences (beyond anaemia) occur in coeliac disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back:
• Fatigue
  • aphthous mouth ulcers
  • bone pain/fractures (calcium/vitamin D deficiency)
  • and subfertility

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the pathognomonic skin manifestation of coeliac disease, and how does it present?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Dermatitis herpetiformis — an intensely itchy, blistering rash on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). "Rash + diarrhoea" = coeliac until proven otherwise. Treat with a gluten-free diet; dapsone gives rapid symptom control (check G6PD first).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: How do adults often present with coeliac disease, and what does this mean for testing?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Subtly or atypically — e.g. "iron-deficiency anaemia not responding to iron" or chronic fatigue. Keep a low threshold to test serology.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the first-line serology test for coeliac disease, and what must always be requested alongside it?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: IgA tissue transglutaminase (IgA tTG). Always request total IgA alongside it (see the IgA deficiency trap). If the IgA tTG is weakly positive, IgA endomysial antibody (EMA) is used next (NICE).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the gold-standard test for coeliac disease, and what does it show?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Duodenal biopsy at OGD: villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytosis + lamina propria lymphocytic infiltrate. Positive serology + positive biopsy usually confirms the diagnosis; biopsy is the preferred route, though a specialist may occasionally diagnose without it when tTG is very high (BSG).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What bloods are relevant in coeliac disease, and what blood-film finding may be seen?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: FBC (anaemia), ferritin, folate, B12, calcium, vitamin D, and LFTs. Blood film: Howell-Jolly bodies (functional hyposplenism).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: Testing trap 1: why must the patient keep eating gluten before coeliac testing?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: The patient must be on a gluten-containing diet for ≥6 weeks — gluten in more than 1 meal every day (NICE) — before serology and biopsy. A gluten-free diet normalises antibodies and heals villi → a false-negative result.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: Testing trap 2: how does IgA deficiency affect coeliac testing, and how is it managed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Coeliac is associated with selective IgA deficiency. If IgA is low, the IgA-tTG will be falsely negative despite active disease. Always check total IgA — if deficient, use IgG-based tests (IgG-EMA, IgG-DGP or IgG-tTG) (NICE).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the treatment for coeliac disease, and how is follow-up done?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: A lifelong gluten-free diet — the only effective treatment. Avoid wheat, barley, rye; oats are usually tolerated if uncontaminated, though a minority still react. Refer to a dietitian with specialist knowledge of coeliac disease, and offer annual review with dietary assessment — serology alone does not confirm that gluten has been excluded (NICE).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: Why is pneumococcal vaccination indicated in coeliac disease, and what is the schedule?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Functional hyposplenism → increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria (Pneumococcus, Hib, Meningococcus). Vaccinate at diagnosis; a 5-yearly pneumococcal booster follows the same logic as other hyposplenic states.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What deficiencies are replaced in coeliac disease, and when is osteoporosis screening done?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Iron, folate, B12, calcium, and vitamin D as indicated. Bone density is assessed with DEXA after diagnosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is the malabsorption anaemia picture in coeliac disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back:
• Iron-deficiency (↓MCV)
  • folate deficiency (↑MCV)
  • B12 deficiency (↑MCV + neurological)
Often a mixed picture.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: Why do osteoporosis/osteomalacia occur in coeliac disease, and what monitoring is used?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Calcium + vitamin D malabsorption → reduced bone density → increased fracture risk. Monitored with DEXA.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What blood-film finding indicates functional hyposplenism in coeliac disease, and what is the consequence?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Howell-Jolly bodies on the blood film (nuclear remnants normally culled by the spleen). It increases infection risk from encapsulated organisms → drives vaccination.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: What is EATL, and why is it significant in coeliac disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma — the key malignancy of coeliac disease. New B-symptoms or weight loss despite a strict gluten-free diet → suspect EATL.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.front: Besides EATL, what other malignancies are associated with coeliac disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.back: Small-bowel adenocarcinoma and oesophageal cancer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is GI motility?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The coordinated muscular movement that propels food through the gut and mixes it with secretions — from swallowing to defecation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the organising principle of GI motility.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The gut has its own nervous system (the enteric nervous system) that runs motility semi-autonomously, modulated by the autonomic system and gut hormones — and each region has a specialised movement pattern for its job (propulsion vs mixing vs storage).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Which muscle layer provides motility, and what lies between its two layers?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The muscularis externa: an inner circular + outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer, with the myenteric plexus between them. The smooth muscle behaves as a syncytium (cells electrically coupled) → coordinated contraction.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe the enteric nervous system and its two plexuses.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
The intrinsic, semi-autonomous 'gut brain' network running motility + secretion. Two plexuses:
  • myenteric (Auerbach's) → motility
  • submucosal (Meissner's) → secretion/blood flow

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How does the autonomic nervous system modulate motility?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Parasympathetic (vagus) → ↑motility ('rest and digest')
  • sympathetic → ↓motility

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What role do gut hormones and pacemaker cells play in motility?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Hormones (gastrin, motilin, CCK etc.) modulate; interstitial cells of Cajal = the pacemakers setting the basic electrical rhythm (generating slow waves — the basal electrical rhythm that sets the pace of contractions).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the ENS point about independence from the CNS.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The gut can run motility independently of the CNS (the ENS has about as many neurons as the spinal cord) — the brain modulates but doesn't generate the basic patterns.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Contrast the two basic movement patterns: peristalsis and segmentation.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Peristalsis: propulsion — a coordinated wave (contraction behind, relaxation ahead) pushes contents forward, throughout the gut
  • Segmentation: mixing — localised contractions churn contents with secretions (no net forward movement), mainly small intestine
Principle: peristalsis moves, segmentation mixes.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe oesophageal motility and its associated disorders.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Swallowing → peristaltic wave; LOS relaxes to admit food. LOS dysfunction → achalasia (fails to relax) or GORD (too lax).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe gastric motility and what regulates emptying.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Receptive relaxation (stores)
  • mixing/grinding (antrum)
  • controlled gastric emptying through the pylorus
Emptying is regulated by duodenal feedback (CCK slows it); gastroparesis = delayed emptying (diabetes).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe small intestine and large intestine motility.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Small intestine: segmentation (mixing) for digestion/absorption + slow peristalsis; the MMC sweeps between meals. Large intestine: slow — haustral churning + mass movements (strong propulsive waves, often post-meal); water absorption + storage; gastrocolic reflex (eating → urge to defecate).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe the defecation reflex and what maintains continence.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Rectal distension → internal sphincter relaxes (involuntary) + voluntary external sphincter control. Continence = the two sphincters.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC), and its drug link?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Between meals, a periodic 'housekeeping' peristaltic wave sweeps residual contents through (stimulated by motilin) → keeps the gut clear; erythromycin mimics motilin → prokinetic.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: List the key GI reflexes and sphincters.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Swallowing reflex (voluntary → involuntary peristalsis + LOS relaxation)
  • receptive relaxation (vagally-mediated stomach relaxation to accommodate food without ↑pressure)
  • gastrocolic reflex (eating → colonic mass movement → post-meal defecation urge)
  • defecation reflex (rectal stretch → internal sphincter relaxes + external voluntary control)
The sphincters: LOS, pyloric, ileocaecal, internal + external anal — each gates flow between segments.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: In motility terms, what causes achalasia and GORD?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Achalasia: LOS fails to relax + absent oesophageal peristalsis → dysphagia (loss of myenteric plexus neurons). GORD: lax/incompetent LOS → acid reflux.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: In motility terms, what are gastroparesis and paralytic ileus?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Gastroparesis: delayed gastric emptying (diabetic autonomic neuropathy) → nausea/bloating; treat with prokinetics. Ileus (paralytic): absent motility post-op/post-inflammation → functional obstruction.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: In motility terms, what is Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Absent enteric ganglia (aganglionic segment) → failure of peristalsis → neonatal obstruction/constipation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Contrast prokinetics and anti-motility drugs.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Prokinetics (metoclopramide, domperidone, erythromycin): ↑motility/gastric emptying. Anti-motility (loperamide): ↓gut motility (diarrhoea — but avoid in inflammatory/bloody, infective diarrhoea).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How much fluid does the GI tract secrete daily, and what does it secrete?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ~7 L of fluid daily — enzymes, acid, bicarbonate, bile, and mucus — to digest food, protect the mucosa, and create the right environment for each digestive step.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the organising principle of GI secretions.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Each region secretes something specific for its job, controlled by a mix of neural (vagal), hormonal (gastrin, CCK, secretin), and local signals — and the three phases of digestion (cephalic, gastric, intestinal) time these secretions to the meal.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What are the major secretions by site (salivary glands, stomach, pancreas, liver/gallbladder, small intestine)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Salivary glands: saliva (amylase, mucus, bicarbonate) — begins starch digestion, lubricates
  • Stomach: acid (HCl), pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, mucus — protein digestion, sterilisation, B12 absorption
  • Pancreas: digestive enzymes + bicarbonate — the main digestive enzymes; neutralises acid
  • Liver/gallbladder: bile — fat emulsification
  • Small intestine: membrane-bound brush-border enzymes, mucus and alkaline fluid — final digestion at the absorptive surface

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What do parietal cells and chief cells secrete, and their roles?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Parietal cells: HCl (acid) + intrinsic factor → acid (digestion/sterilisation) + IF (B12 absorption)
  • Chief cells: pepsinogen → pepsin (in acid) → protein digestion

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What do G cells, mucous cells and ECL cells secrete in the stomach?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• G cells (antrum): gastrin (hormone) → stimulates acid secretion
  • Mucous cells: mucus + bicarbonate → mucosal protection
  • Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells: histamine → stimulates parietal cells

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe the acid secretion mechanism and its three converging stimulatory signals.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
Parietal cells secrete H⁺ via the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase ('proton pump') — stimulated by three converging signals:
  • gastrin (G cells)
  • histamine (ECL cells, via H2 receptors)
  • and ACh (vagus)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Map the acid-lowering drugs to their targets.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• PPIs (omeprazole) block the proton pump (final common step — most powerful)
  • H2 blockers (famotidine) block histamine's contribution
  • vagotomy (historical) cuts the ACh input

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What does intrinsic factor do, and what causes its loss?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Parietal cells make intrinsic factor, essential for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum → loss (autoimmune parietal cell destruction = pernicious anaemia; gastrectomy) → B12 deficiency (macrocytic anaemia).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How is the stomach protected from its own acid, and what disrupts this?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The mucus-bicarbonate barrier + prostaglandins protect the stomach → NSAIDs (block prostaglandins) + H. pylori → peptic ulcers.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What do pancreatic acinar and ductal cells secrete, and their functions?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Acinar cells: digestive enzymes — amylase (carbs), lipase (fat), proteases (trypsin/chymotrypsin — protein)
  • Ductal cells: bicarbonate-rich fluid — neutralises gastric acid entering the duodenum (creates the alkaline pH enzymes need)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Explain the zymogen safety point for pancreatic proteases.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens (e.g. trypsinogen) and activated only in the duodenum (enterokinase → trypsin → activates the rest) → prevents the pancreas digesting itself.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the pancreatitis link, and what is pancreatic exocrine insufficiency?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Premature intra-pancreatic activation of trypsinogen → the pancreas autodigests → acute pancreatitis. Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis) → ↓enzymes → malabsorption + steatorrhoea → treat with enzyme replacement (Creon).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Where is bile made, stored and released, and what do bile salts do?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Made by the liver
  • stored/concentrated in the gallbladder
  • released into the duodenum
Bile salts emulsify fat (break large fat globules into small droplets → ↑surface area for lipase) → essential for fat + fat-soluble vitamin (ADEK) absorption. Bile is also the route for bilirubin excretion; released in response to CCK (fatty meal → gallbladder contraction); the enterohepatic circulation recycles bile salts.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe the three phases of digestion (trigger and effect).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Cephalic: sight/smell/taste/thought of food (vagal) → anticipatory acid + enzyme secretion
  • Gastric: food in the stomach (distension, peptides) → gastrin → acid; peak secretion
  • Intestinal: chyme entering the duodenum → CCK + secretin (regulate pancreas/bile + feedback-inhibit the stomach)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Summarise the key gut hormones controlling secretion (gastrin, CCK, secretin).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Gastrin (G cells) → ↑gastric acid
  • CCK (duodenum, to fat/protein) → ↑pancreatic enzymes + gallbladder contraction + slows gastric emptying
  • Secretin (duodenum, to acid) → ↑pancreatic + biliary bicarbonate (neutralises acid)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the logic of duodenal secretion control.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The duodenum senses acid (→ secretin → bicarbonate to neutralise) and fat/protein (→ CCK → enzymes + bile to digest) → a feedback system matching secretion to need.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: In secretion terms, what causes peptic ulcer/GORD and pernicious anaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Peptic ulcer/GORD: acid vs mucosal defence imbalance (H. pylori, NSAIDs); PPIs block the proton pump, H2 blockers block histamine. Pernicious anaemia: autoimmune loss of parietal cells/intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and what acid-base disturbance does vomiting cause?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Zollinger-Ellison: gastrin-secreting tumour → ↑↑acid → severe/recurrent ulcers. Vomiting: loss of gastric H⁺ → metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is digestion, and which is the absorptive organ?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Digestion breaks the three macronutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, fats — into absorbable units, which are then taken up across the small intestine (the absorptive organ).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the organising principle of digestion and absorption.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Each macronutrient has its own enzyme sequence → final absorbable unit → transport mechanism, and most absorption happens in the small intestine (hugely amplified surface area). Fat is the odd one out (needs bile + a lymphatic route).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How is the small intestine built for absorption, and what is the coeliac link?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Circular folds → villi → microvilli (brush border) → enormously amplified surface area. The brush border carries the final digestive enzymes (disaccharidases, peptidases) → digestion is completed at the absorptive surface. Coeliac link: villous atrophy → loss of surface area → malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe carbohydrate digestion.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Salivary + pancreatic amylase break starch → disaccharides (maltose) + oligosaccharides. Brush-border disaccharidases (maltase, lactase, sucrase) → monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe carbohydrate absorption (which transporters).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Only monosaccharides absorbed: glucose + galactose via SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled, active) into the enterocyte; fructose via GLUT5 (facilitated); then GLUT2 out into the blood.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the lactose intolerance link?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Lactase deficiency → undigested lactose → osmotic diarrhoea + bacterial fermentation (bloating, wind).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe protein digestion.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Stomach: pepsin (from pepsinogen, in acid) begins protein breakdown
  • Pancreas: proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin — activated from zymogens in the duodenum) → peptides
  • Brush-border peptidases → amino acids + di/tripeptides

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe protein absorption.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Amino acids via Na⁺-coupled transporters; di/tripeptides via PepT1 (H⁺-coupled) → broken down to amino acids inside the enterocyte → into blood. The pancreas does the bulk of protein digestion → pancreatic insufficiency → protein (+ fat) malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe fat digestion (emulsification, digestion, micelle formation, absorption).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Emulsification: bile salts (liver/gallbladder, CCK-released) break fat globules into small droplets → ↑surface area
  • Digestion: pancreatic lipase → monoglycerides + free fatty acids
  • Micelle formation: bile salts package these into micelles → ferry them to the brush border
  • Absorption: fatty acids/monoglycerides diffuse into the enterocyte → re-esterified into triglycerides → packaged into chylomicrons

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the lymphatic route for fat, and how does it differ from carbs/proteins?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Chylomicrons are too big for capillaries → enter the lymphatics (lacteals) → thoracic duct → blood, whereas carbs/proteins go straight into the portal blood. The exception: short- and medium-chain fatty acids also pass straight into the portal blood — the basis of MCT feeds in fat malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How are fat-soluble vitamins absorbed, and what results from fat malabsorption?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ADEK are absorbed with fat (in micelles) → fat malabsorption → ADEK deficiency.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is steatorrhoea, and what are the three mechanisms that cause it?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
Fatty, pale, floating, offensive stool — the endpoint of fat maldigestion/malabsorption. Mechanisms:
  • ↓bile (obstruction, cholestasis, bile-salt malabsorption) → can't emulsify
  • ↓lipase (pancreatic insufficiency, CF) → can't digest
  • ↓surface (coeliac, Crohn's) → can't absorb

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Where are iron and folate absorbed, and their clinical links?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Iron: duodenum (+ proximal jejunum) → coeliac/duodenal disease → iron deficiency
  • Folate: duodenum + proximal jejunum

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Where are B12 and bile salts absorbed, and their clinical links?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• B12: terminal ileum (needs intrinsic factor) → terminal ileal disease/resection (Crohn's) or ↓IF (pernicious anaemia) → B12 deficiency
  • Bile salts: terminal ileum (recycled — enterohepatic circulation) → terminal ileal disease → bile salt malabsorption → diarrhoea + fat malabsorption

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: In digestion/absorption terms, what is the mechanism of coeliac disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Gluten → villous atrophy → ↓surface → malabsorption (iron, folate, fat → steatorrhoea, weight loss).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Why is the gut described as the largest endocrine organ?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Scattered enteroendocrine cells in the mucosa release hormones that coordinate digestion, secretion, motility, and appetite.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the organising principle of gut hormones.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Food in the gut lumen → stimulates a specific cell → releases a hormone → that hormone prepares the next part of the GI tract for what's coming (feed-forward control). Most act in a logical pairing (the stimulus and the response make physiological sense).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: For gastrin: which cell/site, stimulus and main action?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: G cells — gastric antrum. Stimulus: peptides/amino acids in stomach, gastric distension, vagus. Main action: ↑gastric acid (parietal cells) + mucosal growth.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: For CCK: which cell/site, stimulus and main action?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: I cells — duodenum/jejunum. Stimulus: fat + protein in duodenum. Main action: gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzyme secretion + satiety; slows gastric emptying.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: For secretin: which cell/site, stimulus and main action?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: S cells — duodenum. Stimulus: acid (low pH) in duodenum. Main action: pancreatic + biliary bicarbonate (neutralises acid); ↓gastric acid.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: For incretins (GIP, GLP-1): which cells/site, stimulus and main action?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: K cells (GIP, duodenum) & L cells (GLP-1, ileum/colon). Stimulus: glucose/nutrients in gut lumen. Main action: ↑insulin from the pancreas (the incretin effect).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the gut hormone memory hook.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• GaStrin from antrum → acid
  • CCK = cholecystokinin, literally "move the gall-bladder" — fat/protein → bile + pancreatic enzymes
  • Secretin for acid → biScarbonate
  • incretins → insulin

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe gastrin (the acid driver) and its regulation.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: From G cells in the antrum → drives parietal cell acid secretion (directly + via histamine from ECL cells) and stimulates mucosal growth. Inhibited by low pH (negative feedback) and somatostatin.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and how does it present?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: A gastrinoma (gastrin-secreting tumour, often pancreatic/duodenal) → unregulated acid → multiple/refractory peptic ulcers (incl. atypical sites), diarrhoea. Think of it with recurrent ulcers despite PPI / ulcers in odd places.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the pairing logic of CCK and secretin (the duodenal pair).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• CCK responds to fat + protein → contracts the gallbladder (delivers bile to emulsify fat) + releases pancreatic enzymes + signals satiety + slows gastric emptying
  • Secretin responds to acid → releases bicarbonate from pancreas/bile ducts + turns down gastric acid
The stimulus always predicts the response.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Explain the incretin effect and GLP-1's additional actions.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Oral glucose triggers more insulin than the same glucose given IV — because the gut releases GIP + GLP-1, which prime the β cells as nutrients arrive, amplifying glucose-stimulated insulin release rather than triggering insulin on their own. GLP-1 also: ↓glucagon, slows gastric emptying, promotes satiety → weight loss. Both are rapidly broken down by DPP-4.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How is the incretin system exploited pharmacologically in T2DM?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide — resist DPP-4) → ↑insulin, satiety, weight loss
  • DPP-4 inhibitors ('gliptins', e.g. sitagliptin) → block breakdown → ↑endogenous incretins
Glucose-dependent action → low hypo risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: For ghrelin and motilin: source and action/clinical hook.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Ghrelin (stomach fundus): 'hunger hormone' — ↑ before meals, drives appetite; falls after eating
  • Motilin (small intestine): drives the MMC (the 'housekeeper' sweep between meals); erythromycin is a motilin agonist (prokinetic)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: For somatostatin: source, action and drug analogue with uses.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: D cells (gut + pancreas): universal inhibitor — turns off acid, gut hormones, pancreatic/GI secretions. Drug analogue = octreotide (variceal bleeds, acromegaly, neuroendocrine tumours/carcinoid).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: For leptin and PYY: source and action.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Leptin (adipose tissue): satiety / long-term energy stores — signals fullness to the hypothalamus; obesity = leptin resistance
  • PYY (L cells, ileum/colon): released after meals → satiety + slows GI transit ('ileal brake')

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Contrast the short vs long game of appetite regulation.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Hunger (↑appetite): ghrelin (from the empty stomach) → stimulates the hypothalamus
  • Satiety (↓appetite): CCK, GLP-1, PYY (released as food arrives — short-term, meal-to-meal) and leptin (from fat stores — long-term energy balance)
All converge on the hypothalamus (arcuate nucleus) to balance intake against energy stores.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the obesity/therapeutics link for appetite hormones?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Bariatric surgery and GLP-1 agonists work partly by shifting these signals (↑satiety, ↓ghrelin effect) → less intake.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is carcinoid syndrome, and how is it treated?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: A neuroendocrine tumour secreting vasoactive substances (serotonin) → flushing, diarrhoea — treated with octreotide.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Why is erythromycin used as a prokinetic?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: It is a motilin-receptor agonist → stimulates gastric emptying (e.g. gastroparesis, before endoscopy).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the liver's overall role, and how does it receive gut blood?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The body's central metabolic and detoxifying organ — it processes everything absorbed into the portal blood from the gut (via the portal vein), synthesises key proteins, stores nutrients, metabolises drugs, and excretes waste.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the organising principle of liver function.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The liver has a handful of core functions — metabolism, synthesis, storage, detoxification, and excretion — and liver disease is understood as the loss of these functions (so LFTs, the bleeding tendency, jaundice, and encephalopathy all become derivable).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe the liver's dual blood supply and its 'first-pass' significance.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Portal vein (~75%, nutrient-rich blood straight from the gut) + hepatic artery (~25%, oxygenated) → the liver is the first organ to process everything absorbed into the portal blood ('first-pass'). Long-chain fats bypass this, entering the lymphatics as chylomicrons. Orally-absorbed drugs/nutrients hit the liver first → first-pass metabolism → why some drugs have low oral bioavailability.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What do hepatocytes and Kupffer cells do?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Hepatocytes do the metabolic work; Kupffer cells (resident macrophages) clear bacteria/debris from portal blood.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: List the five core functions of the liver and what it does for each.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Metabolism: carbohydrate, fat, protein metabolism (the central metabolic hub)
  • Synthesis: albumin, clotting factors, bile, lipoproteins, acute-phase proteins
  • Storage: glycogen, vitamins (A, D, B12, K), iron, copper
  • Detoxification: drugs (CYP450), ammonia → urea, hormones, bilirubin
  • Excretion: bilirubin + bile salts (into bile)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the liver's role in carbohydrate metabolism?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Central to glucose homeostasis — glycogen storage (fed state), glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis (fasted state) → maintains blood glucose.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the liver's role in fat metabolism, and what causes fatty liver?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Fatty acid oxidation
  • ketogenesis (fasting fuel)
  • cholesterol + lipoprotein synthesis (VLDL)
fat accumulation → fatty liver.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the liver's role in protein metabolism?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Transamination/deamination of amino acids; the urea cycle (converts toxic ammonia → urea for excretion).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How does liver failure disrupt metabolism clinically?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: It disrupts all metabolic functions → hypoglycaemia (↓gluconeogenesis) and the metabolic derangements of liver failure.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is albumin's role, and what does its loss cause?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The main plasma protein → maintains oncotic pressure + carries drugs/hormones. Liver failure → ↓albumin → oedema/ascites (↓oncotic pressure).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Which clotting factors does the liver make, and why is PT/INR the best synthetic marker?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The liver makes almost all clotting factors (including the vitamin-K-dependent II, VII, IX, X + protein C/S). Liver failure → ↓clotting factors → bleeding tendency → prolonged PT/INR, the best marker of synthetic liver function (rises early, as factor VII has a short half-life) — provided vitamin K stores are adequate. In cholestasis, vitamin K malabsorption also prolongs the PT, but that corrects with parenteral vitamin K.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How does the liver handle drug metabolism, and what is the clinical relevance?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: CYP450 (Phase I) + conjugation (Phase II) → makes drugs water-soluble for excretion; the basis of hepatic drug clearance + interactions. In liver failure, ↓CYP450 → altered drug metabolism (hepatic dose adjustment).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe the ammonia-urea pathway and the consequence of its failure.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Gut bacteria + protein metabolism produce ammonia (neurotoxic) → the liver converts it to urea (excreted renally). Liver failure → ↓ammonia clearance → ↑ammonia → hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis, coma) → treated with lactulose (traps ammonia in the gut) + rifaximin (↓ammonia-producing gut bacteria).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How does the liver's handling of hormones explain signs of liver failure?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The liver clears hormones (e.g. oestrogen — why liver failure → gynaecomastia/spider naevi) and conjugates bilirubin.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What do ALT + AST reflect on LFTs, and when are they raised?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ALT + AST (transaminases) reflect hepatocyte damage (released from damaged cells) → ↑↑ in hepatocellular injury (hepatitis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What do ALP + GGT reflect on LFTs, and when are they raised?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ALP + GGT reflect biliary/cholestasis → ↑↑ in cholestasis/obstruction (GGT confirms the ALP is hepatic).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What do bilirubin, albumin and PT/INR reflect on LFTs?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Bilirubin: excretory function → ↑ in jaundice
  • Albumin: synthetic function (chronic) → ↓ in chronic liver disease, but it is also a negative acute-phase protein, so it falls in inflammation/sepsis, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition — a low albumin is not specific to liver disease
  • PT/INR: synthetic function (acute) → ↑ in liver failure (↓clotting factors)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the key LFT interpretation point (damage vs function).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ALT/AST = hepatocellular (damage) vs ALP/GGT = cholestatic (obstruction) — the pattern tells you the type of liver problem; albumin + PT/INR = actual function (transaminases tell you about damage, not function).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Why do liver failure patients develop spider naevi and gynaecomastia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ↓oestrogen clearance by the failing liver.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is bilirubin, and what does tracking its journey explain?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The breakdown product of haemoglobin — tracking its journey from red cell to bile explains jaundice and how to classify its cause.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the organising principle of bilirubin metabolism.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Bilirubin passes through three stages — production (from haem) → conjugation (in the liver) → excretion (via bile/gut) — and jaundice is classified by where in this pathway the problem lies: pre-hepatic, hepatic, or post-hepatic.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe production and transport of bilirubin (stages 1-2).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Production: old red cells broken down → haem → biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin (in the spleen/reticuloendothelial system)
  • Transport: unconjugated bilirubin (water-insoluble) travels bound to albumin (in blood)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe conjugation and excretion of bilirubin (stages 3-4).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Conjugation: liver enzyme UDP-glucuronyl transferase conjugates it → conjugated bilirubin (water-soluble) in hepatocytes
  • Excretion: conjugated bilirubin secreted into bile → gut (bile → duodenum)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe the gut conversion of bilirubin (stage 5).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Gut bacteria → urobilinogen → stercobilin (brown stool) + some reabsorbed → urine (urobilin), in the intestine.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Contrast unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin (solubility, carriage, urine).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Unconjugated: water-insoluble (lipid-soluble), bound to albumin, NOT in urine (albumin-bound, can't be filtered)
  • Conjugated: water-soluble, free (soluble), YES in urine (→ dark urine)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Contrast unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin (BBB crossing, when raised).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Unconjugated: crosses the BBB (lipid-soluble → kernicterus risk in neonates); raised in pre-hepatic (haemolysis) + Gilbert's
  • Conjugated: does NOT cross the BBB; raised in hepatic + post-hepatic (obstruction)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the key concept explaining why conjugated bilirubin appears in urine but unconjugated doesn't.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Conjugation makes bilirubin water-soluble → so conjugated bilirubin can appear in urine (dark urine), unconjugated cannot (it's albumin-bound). This is the basis of distinguishing the jaundice types.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe pre-hepatic jaundice (problem, bilirubin type, key features).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Problem: ↑production (too much haem breakdown)
  • Bilirubin: unconjugated
  • Key features: haemolysis → ↑unconjugated; urine not dark (no bilirubin in urine, though urobilinogen may be ↑), stool normal; ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, ↑reticulocytes

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe hepatic jaundice (problem, bilirubin type, key features).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Problem: liver can't conjugate/process
  • Bilirubin: mixed (unconjugated + conjugated)
  • Key features: hepatitis, cirrhosis; ↑ALT/AST
Isolated conjugation defects (Gilbert's) are the exception — they raise unconjugated bilirubin only.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice (problem, bilirubin type, key features).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Problem: can't excrete (bile flow blocked)
  • Bilirubin: conjugated
  • Key features: gallstones, tumour; dark urine + pale stools + itch; ↑ALP/GGT

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Explain the post-hepatic obstruction pattern (dark urine, pale stools, itch, ALP/GGT).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
Conjugated bilirubin ↑ →
  • dark urine (soluble bilirubin filtered)
  • pale stools (no bilirubin reaching gut → no stercobilin)
  • itch (bile salts)
  • ↑ALP/GGT (cholestatic)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Explain the pre-hepatic (haemolysis) pattern regarding urine and stool.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Unconjugated ↑ → jaundice but the urine is not dark and the stool is normal (unconjugated bilirubin can't be excreted in urine, though urobilinogen may rise; conjugation/excretion downstream is intact) + the haemolysis labs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is Gilbert's syndrome, and how is it managed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: A benign mild reduction in conjugation (mild ↓UDP-glucuronyl transferase) → mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, often noticed as jaundice during illness/fasting/stress → reassurance only.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is Crigler-Najjar syndrome?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Severe/absent conjugation enzyme → ↑↑unconjugated (severe).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Explain neonatal jaundice and its treatment.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Immature liver conjugation + high red cell turnover → unconjugated → risk of kernicterus (unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature BBB → brain damage) → treated with phototherapy (converts bilirubin to a water-soluble form).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What defect underlies Dubin-Johnson / Rotor syndrome?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ↓ hepatic handling of conjugated bilirubin (rare, benign) → ↑conjugated.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the urine/stool clues for classifying jaundice.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Dark urine = conjugated
  • pale stool = obstruction
  • urine not dark with normal stool = pre-hepatic

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What are bile's two jobs, and what does disrupting bile cause?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Fat digestion (bile salts) and excretion (bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs). The enterohepatic circulation recycles bile salts so the body doesn't make them fresh each meal. Disrupting bile flow or composition causes gallstones, fat malabsorption, and cholestasis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: List the components of bile and their roles.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Bile salts/acids: emulsify fat (the digestive function) — the main players
  • Bilirubin: excretory waste (from haem breakdown)
  • Cholesterol: excreted in bile; excess → gallstones
  • Phospholipids (lecithin): keep cholesterol soluble in bile
  • Bicarbonate/water: (from ductal cells) alkaline fluid

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the gallstone balance.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Bile salts + phospholipids keep cholesterol dissolved; if cholesterol is in excess (or bile salts ↓) → cholesterol precipitates → gallstones.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Describe bile production, storage and release.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Made continuously by hepatocytes → secreted into bile canaliculi → bile ducts
  • Stored + concentrated in the gallbladder between meals (water reabsorbed → concentrated up to ~10×)
  • Released into the duodenum when needed: a fatty meal → CCK → gallbladder contracts + sphincter of Oddi relaxes → bile flows into the duodenum

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is biliary colic, and what triggers it?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: A gallstone obstructing the cystic/common bile duct → pain when the gallbladder contracts against the obstruction, especially after fatty meals (CCK-driven).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Why are bile salts amphipathic, and what does this let them do?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: They have water- and fat-soluble ends → they emulsify fat (break large globules into small droplets → ↑surface area for lipase) and form micelles that ferry fat-breakdown products to the enterocyte. Essential for absorbing fat + the fat-soluble vitamins ADEK.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the bile malabsorption link?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ↓bile (obstruction, cholestasis, bile-salt loss) → fat malabsorption → steatorrhoea + ADEK deficiency.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: State the principle of the enterohepatic circulation.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Bile salts released into the duodenum → emulsify fat → travel down the gut → reabsorbed in the terminal ileum → return to the liver via the portal vein → re-secreted into bile.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How efficient is the enterohepatic circulation?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: The bile salt pool recirculates several times per meal; only ~5% is lost in faeces (and replaced by new hepatic synthesis) → the body conserves bile salts rather than making them fresh each time.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Why is the terminal ileum the key site for bile salts, and what happens in terminal ileal disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum (same site as B12) → so terminal ileal disease/resection (Crohn's) → bile salt malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What are the two consequences of bile salt malabsorption from terminal ileal disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Bile salts spill into the colon → bile-acid diarrhoea (they irritate the colon) → treated with colestyramine (binds bile acids)
  • depleted bile salt pool → fat malabsorption + ↑gallstone risk (less bile salt to keep cholesterol soluble)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What substances does bile excrete that the kidney can't handle?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back:
• Bilirubin
  • cholesterol
  • drugs/metabolites
  • copper (→ Wilson's disease if it accumulates)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: Explain the obstruction link for bile flow.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Blocked bile flow (gallstone, tumour) → conjugated bilirubin can't be excreted → obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools) + bile salts back up → itch (pruritus).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How do gallstones form, and when is the risk increased?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: Cholesterol excess (or ↓bile salts/lecithin) → precipitation; risk ↑ with terminal ileal disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: How is colestyramine used clinically?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: It binds bile acids (used for bile-acid diarrhoea, and pruritus of cholestasis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.front: What is the bile-related mechanism of Wilson's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.back: ↓biliary copper excretion → copper accumulation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is IBS, and what defines it pathologically?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Irritable Bowel Syndrome — a functional bowel disorder. Symptoms arise from abnormal gut functioning with no identifiable structural or organic disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is the central two-step fork in diagnosing IBS?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back:
• Step 1: Exclude organic causes (red flags + investigations)
  • Step 2: Diagnose positively on symptom criteria
IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion — but made positively, not just by default.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is the IBS triad?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back:
• Intestinal discomfort
  • bowel habit change
  • and stool abnormality

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: How do IBS, IBD, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer relate to one another?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back:
• IBD is the organic mirror — IBS is what remains when inflammation is excluded
  • Coeliac disease is the key mimic — always exclude
  • Colorectal cancer is the red-flag concern in any bowel habit change

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: Describe the abdominal pain of IBS.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Relieved by defecation, worse after eating. Cramping, colicky, and typically lower abdomen.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: Describe the altered bowel habit of IBS.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Fluctuating — diarrhoea, constipation, or alternating. With urgency, straining, and a sensation of incomplete emptying.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: Describe the bloating/distension of IBS, and what is notably absent from the stool.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Often worse after eating, relieved partially by defecation. Passage of mucus — but no blood.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is the overall IBS symptom pattern, and what is the key clinical rule?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Chronic, relapsing, and without alarm features. Pain relieved by defecation + a fluctuating habit without weight loss/bleeding = functional until red flags say otherwise.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: Which red flags exclude IBS and mandate investigation, and what is the concern for each?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back:
• Rectal bleeding (IBD, colorectal cancer)
  • unexplained weight loss (cancer, IBD, coeliac)
  • anaemia (cancer, coeliac, IBD)
  • a change in bowel habit to looser/more frequent stools for over 6 weeks aged over 60, or nocturnal symptoms (organic pathology)
  • and a family history of bowel or ovarian cancer
Any one mandates referral to secondary care (NICE).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What four features does IBS NOT cause, and what do they imply if present?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: IBS does not cause weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, or nocturnal symptoms. Any of these mandates referral to secondary care for investigation of IBD, cancer or coeliac disease (NICE). A red flag appearing later, during follow-up, prompts the same.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What should investigation results show in IBS, and what is their purpose?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: All results should be normal in IBS — the purpose is to exclude organic mimics, not to diagnose IBS itself.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What do FBC + CRP/ESR show in IBS, and why are they useful?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Normal in IBS. Raised CRP/ESR points away from IBS — think IBD or another organic cause. FBC checks for anaemia (cancer, coeliac, IBD).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is the role of faecal calprotectin in IBS, and how is it interpreted?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: The IBS vs IBD discriminator. Raised = mucosal inflammation (IBD); normal = functional disorder (IBS). Highly sensitive for active colonic inflammation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: Why is coeliac serology (IgA tTG) mandatory before diagnosing IBS?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Coeliac is a treatable mimic with an identical GI presentation, so IgA tTG is mandatory before diagnosing IBS.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: In whom is CA125 checked in the context of IBS-type symptoms?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: In any woman aged 50 or over with IBS-type symptoms starting in the last 12 months — IBS rarely presents for the first time at this age (NICE). Bloating and abdominal symptoms overlap with IBS. Do not miss it.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is the core diagnostic criterion for IBS?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: ≥6 months of abdominal pain/discomfort that is relieved by defecation OR associated with altered stool frequency or form, PLUS ≥2 supporting features.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What are the supporting features (≥2 required) for an IBS diagnosis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back:
• Straining/urgency/incomplete emptying
  • bloating or distension
  • symptoms worse after eating
  • and passage of mucus

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What first-line lifestyle and dietary measures are used in IBS?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back:
• Regular unhurried meals
  • avoid skipping
  • adequate fluid intake
  • limit caffeine, alcohol, and fizzy drinks
  • and adjust fibre — if increasing it use soluble fibre (ispaghula, oats) and discourage insoluble fibre such as bran (NICE)

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is the low-FODMAP diet, and what is its place in IBS management?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: A diet limiting fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols. It is second-line dietary management, given only by a professional with expertise in dietary management (NICE).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.front: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for pain/spasm in IBS?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.back: Antispasmodics — mebeverine, hyoscine butylbromide, or peppermint oil.
